title: Where variables live
summary: A name set inside a function is local: it exists only while the function runs and hides any outside name with the same spelling. Reading an outside name works, but setting one inside makes Python treat it as local everywhere in the function. Pass values in and return them, instead of reaching outside. A list or dict default is made once and shared by every call: use None.
objectives: Tell local names from global ones.
Explain UnboundLocalError and fix it by passing and returning.
Know that a list passed in can be changed by the function.
Avoid list and dict defaults with None.

slides.h: By the end: a loan counter that counts
slides.say: Meera’s counter of today’s loans crashes on the first book. By the end of this lesson you’ll see why, and fix it the clean way.
points: Names made inside a function are **local**: they vanish when it returns.
Names made at the top of the program are **global**.
A local name hides a global one with the same spelling.

visual.text:
x = 10

def f():
    x = 5
    return x

print(f(), x)
visual.why: The x inside f is a different, local x.

terms: a name that belongs to one run of a function
a name made at the top level of the program

slides.say: If a function assigns to a name anywhere in its body, that name is local for the whole function, so reading it before the assignment fails.
points: `global count` would allow it, but makes code hard to test.
Better: take the value as a parameter and return the new one.

visual.wrong:
count = 0

def borrow(title):
    count = count + 1
    print(f"Borrowed {title} ({count} today)")

borrow("Godan")
visual.err:
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "main.py", line 7, in <module>
    borrow("Godan")
  File "main.py", line 4, in borrow
    count = count + 1
UnboundLocalError: cannot access local variable 'count' where it is not associated with a value
visual.right:
count = 0

def borrow(title, count):
    count = count + 1
    print(f"Borrowed {title} ({count} today)")
    return count

count = borrow("Godan", count)
visual.what: UnboundLocalError: count is assigned inside borrow, so it is local there, and it has no value yet when count + 1 runs.

check.q: Inside a function, `total = total + 1` with total only set outside gives…
options: it adds 1 to the outside total

lecture.title: Shared lists and the mutable default

slides.h: A list passed in is the same list
slides.say: Passing a list doesn’t copy it. If the function appends to it, the caller’s list changes too. Sometimes that’s what you want; say so in the name, like `add_loan(loans, ...)`.
points: Numbers and text can’t change, so this only matters for lists, dicts and sets.
p: Passing a list doesn’t copy it. If the function appends to it, the caller’s list changes too. Sometimes that’s what you want; say so in the name, like `add_loan(loans, ...)`.
Numbers and text can’t change, so this only matters for lists, dicts and sets.

visual.text:
def add_loan(loans, title):
    loans.append(title)

today = []
add_loan(today, "Godan")
add_loan(today, "The Guide")
print(today)

slides.say: A default is made once, when the def runs, not at each call. A list default is the **same list** every time.
points: Use `None` as the default and make the list inside.
p: A default is made once, when the def runs, not at each call. A list default is the **same list** every time.
Use `None` as the default and make the list inside.

visual.wrong:
def add_tag(tag, tags=[]):
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags

print(add_tag("fiction"))
print(add_tag("history"))
visual.right:
def add_tag(tag, tags=None):
    if tags is None:
        tags = []
    tags.append(tag)
    return tags

print(add_tag("fiction"))
print(add_tag("history"))
visual.what: The second call prints ['fiction', 'history']: both calls share one list.

options: A [] default is made once and shared by every call

bank.code:

    xs = []

clear(nums)

points: Names set in a function are local; they vanish when it returns.
Setting a name inside makes it local everywhere in the function: UnboundLocalError.
Pass values in, return them out; avoid global.
Lists passed in can be changed; never use [] or {} as a default: use None.
recap.cheat: def f(x, items=None): if items is None: items = []

cards.back: It assigns to a name it also reads: pass the value in and return it.
Defaults are made once: use None and make the list inside.

cards.back: No: the function can change the caller’s list.
